raw_case_text:
A 6-year-old girl presented to the ENT clinic for 3-month history of a slowly growing left postauricular cervical mass. The patient's family denied any history of fever, pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, or weight loss. The girl resides in a rural area of Lebanon, where livestock farming is common and sanitation infrastructure is limited. Her family is of low socioeconomic status and lives in close proximity to domesticated animals, including sheep and dogs. The physical exam revealed an oval-shaped, soft, nontender mass. The overlying skin showed no signs of inflammation, and no cervical lymphadenopathy was detected. Routine laboratory testing was unremarkable. A neck ultrasound was performed next, and it showed a well-circumscribed anechoic cystic mass measuring 34.7 x 28.6 mm in the left postauricular area. No cervical adenopathy was identified. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan was subsequently performed to better delineate the anatomic relationships of the lesion, assess any soft tissue component or calcifications, and evaluate for potential invasion or compression of adjacent structures. It showed a level V unilocular cystic neck mass. It was seen posterior to the parotid gland and to sternocleidomastoid muscle, anterior to trapezius muscle, and independent from the carotid space. The mass was not enhancing, very well circumscribed, with no soft tissue component. While MRI is superior to CT in soft tissue characterization and avoids radiation, CT was chosen due to faster accessibility and high-resolution depiction of bone and soft tissue anatomy, offering rapid, detailed visualization of the lesion's extent and relation to vital structures. The mass looked benign, but it has been present for some time, slowly growing, and so the decision was taken to have it removed (Figure 1).
Complete resection of the cyst including tissues surrounding the cyst was performed. During the procedure, the cyst partially ruptured, and it was found to contain clear fluid and surrounded by a white germinal membrane. Since the lesion did not raise oncologic concern, and given the characteristic features seen intraoperatively, which raised the suspicion for hydatid disease, a frozen section was not deemed necessary. The mass was sent for final pathology, which revealed an echinococcal cyst (hydatid cyst) (Figures 2 and 3).
Further workup was done, including a chest radiograph and a liver ultrasound, both of which were unremarkable. The postoperative course was uneventful. The patient was referred to an infectious disease specialist and was started on albendazole 400 mg/day for 3 months, due to intraoperative rupture of the cyst, which increases the risk of microscopic spillage and recurrence. Prolonged therapy in such cases has been recommended, despite the known risk of hepatotoxicity. Liver function was monitored regularly, and the patient remained stable throughout the treatment. At 3-month follow-up, the patient remained disease free.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 6-year-old girl presented with a 3-month history of a slowly enlarging left postauricular neck mass.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child was brought to the ENT clinic with a painless, slowly growing mass in the left postauricular cervical region noticed 3 months earlier.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resided in a rural livestock-farming area of Lebanon with limited sanitation and close household proximity to sheep and dogs.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painless left postauricular mass; negative for fever, pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: An oval-shaped, soft, non-tender mass was palpated in the left postauricular region without overlying skin inflammation or cervical lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests were unremarkable. Neck ultrasound revealed a well-circumscribed 34.7 x 28.6 mm anechoic cystic mass in the left postauricular region without cervical lymphadenopathy. Postoperative chest radiograph and liver ultrasound were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced neck CT demonstrated a well-circumscribed, non-enhancing unilocular cystic mass without soft tissue components or calcifications in left cervical level V (posterior to the parotid gland and sternocleidomastoid muscle, anterior to the trapezius, and separate from the carotid space). During complete surgical excision, the cyst partially ruptured, releasing clear fluid and a white germinal membrane; final histopathology confirmed an echinococcal (hydatid) cyst.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary isolated left postauricular (level V cervical) hydatid cyst, confirmed by intraoperative identification of clear fluid and white germinal membrane and final histopathology. Following complete surgical excision complicated by partial intraoperative rupture, the patient was treated with oral albendazole 400 mg/day for 3 months with regular liver function monitoring, remaining stable and disease-free at 3-month follow-up.
